passages.c: From the Meditations, the private notebook of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, in Meric Casaubon’s 1634 translation. “Thou” is Marcus addressing himself.
passages.q: Where can a person find real rest, according to Marcus?
p: They seek for themselves private retiring places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself art wont to long much after such places. But all this thou must know proceeds from simplicity in the highest degree. At what time soever thou wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and free from all businesses. A man cannot any whither retire better than to his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such things within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity. By tranquillity I understand a decent orderly disposition and carriage, free from all confusion and tumultuousness.

Afford then thyself this retiring continually, and thereby refresh and renew thyself. Let these precepts be brief and fundamental, which as soon as thou dost call them to mind, may suffice thee to purge thy soul throughly, and to send thee away well pleased with those things whatsoever they be, which now again after this short withdrawing of thy soul into herself thou dost return unto. For what is it that thou art offended at? Can it be at the wickedness of men, when thou dost call to mind this conclusion, that all reasonable creatures are made one for another? and that it is part of justice to bear with them? and that it is against their wills that they offend? and how many already, who once likewise prosecuted their enmities, suspected, hated, and fiercely contended, are now long ago stretched out, and reduced unto ashes?

It is time for thee to make an end. As for those things which among the common chances of the world happen unto thee as thy particular lot and portion, canst thou be displeased with any of them, when thou dost call that our ordinary dilemma to mind, either a providence, or Democritus his atoms; and with it, whatsoever we brought to prove that the whole world is as it were one city?
g: People seek retreats in the country or by the sea, but that is naive: at any moment you can retire into your own soul and find calm order.

So take this retreat often, with a few short principles that send you back content; if men’s wickedness bothers you, remember we exist for one another, they do wrong unwillingly, and the quarrelsome dead are ashes now.
Enough. Whatever fate hands you, remember the choice: providence or random atoms; either way the world is like one city.
k: You can retire into your own soul at any moment; no place is quieter.
Keep a few brief principles ready to restore calm.
On others’ wrongs: we are made for one another, they offend unwillingly, and all enmities end in ashes.

passages.w: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History
passages.c: The opening of Carlyle’s first lecture On Heroes, delivered in 1840 and published in 1841. It is the classic statement of the “great man” theory of history.
passages.q: What, according to Carlyle, is history really the history of?
p: We have undertaken to discourse here for a little on Great Men, their manner of appearance in our world's business, how they have shaped themselves in the world's history, what ideas men formed of them, what work they did;--on Heroes, namely, and on their reception and performance; what I call Hero-worship and the Heroic in human affairs. Too evidently this is a large topic; deserving quite other treatment than we can expect to give it at present. A large topic; indeed, an illimitable one; wide as Universal History itself. For, as I take it, Universal History, the history of what man has accomplished in this world, is at bottom the History of the Great Men who have worked here.

They were the leaders of men, these great ones; the modellers, patterns, and in a wide sense creators, of whatsoever the general mass of men contrived to do or to attain; all things that we see standing accomplished in the world are properly the outer material result, the practical realization and embodiment, of Thoughts that dwelt in the Great Men sent into the world: the soul of the whole world's history, it may justly be considered, were the history of these. Too clearly it is a topic we shall do no justice to in this place!
g: Carlyle will discuss great men: how they appeared, what people thought of them and what they did, a vast topic, because universal history is at bottom the history of great men.
They led, modelled and created whatever the mass of people achieved; everything accomplished is the outward realisation of their thoughts, the soul of world history.
k: Universal history is at bottom the history of the great men who have worked here.
Great men were the leaders, models and creators of what the mass of men achieved.
All accomplishment is the outer realisation of thoughts in great men.

mc.s: What is Carlyle’s thesis?
o: History is shaped mainly by the thoughts and actions of exceptional individuals
History is shaped mainly by economic forces
Great men are made by their times
mc.e: “Universal History… is at bottom the History of the Great Men who have worked here.”

mc.s: Which historian would most directly challenge Carlyle?
o: One who argues events are driven by broad social and economic forces, not individuals
One who writes a biography of Napoleon
mc.e: The others fit his view. Only the first denies that great men are the soul of history.

mc.s: How does Carlyle see the role of ordinary people?
o: As largely following and carrying out what great men conceived
As the true drivers of history
As equal partners with great men
mc.e: Great men were “the modellers, patterns” of “whatsoever the general mass of men contrived to do”.

v.d: The topic is “a large topic; indeed, an illimitable one”.

o: a visible, concrete form of an idea
v.d: Achievements are “the practical realization and embodiment, of Thoughts”.

passages.c: From The Souls of Black Folk (1903), chapter I, “Of Our Spiritual Strivings”. Du Bois writes about Black Americans forty years after emancipation, in the language of his time.
passages.q: What is double-consciousness, and what does Du Bois want instead?
p: After the Egyptian and Indian, the Greek and Roman, the Teuton and Mongolian, the Negro is a sort of seventh son, born with a veil, and gifted with second-sight in this American world,--a world which yields him no true self-consciousness, but only lets him see himself through the revelation of the other world. It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity. One ever feels his twoness,--an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder.

The history of the American Negro is the history of this strife,--this longing to attain self-conscious manhood, to merge his double self into a better and truer self. In this merging he wishes neither of the older selves to be lost. He would not Africanize America, for America has too much to teach the world and Africa. He would not bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism, for he knows that Negro blood has a message for the world. He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American, without being cursed and spit upon by his fellows, without having the doors of Opportunity closed roughly in his face.
g: Black Americans, Du Bois says, live with “double-consciousness”: always seeing themselves through the contemptuous eyes of others, feeling two warring identities, American and Negro, in one body.
Their history is the struggle to merge these into a truer self without losing either: to be both Black and American without being cursed or shut out of opportunity.
k: Double-consciousness: always seeing oneself through the eyes of a contemptuous world.
“Twoness”: two souls, two unreconciled strivings, in one body.
The aim is to be both, losing neither self, without the doors of opportunity being closed.

mc.s: What does Du Bois want?
o: To be both Black and American, fully, without being scorned or shut out
To give up Black identity and blend in
mc.e: “He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American.”

mc.s: What makes double-consciousness painful, as he describes it?
o: One’s sense of self is measured by a world that looks on with contempt and pity
mc.e: “Measuring one’s soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity.”

mc.s: How does the second paragraph relate to the first?
o: It turns the description of a divided self into a statement of the goal: merging both selves
It changes the subject to Africa
mc.e: From the strife of twoness to the longing “to merge his double self into a better and truer self”.

v.d: Only dogged strength keeps the body “from being torn asunder”.
“Two unreconciled strivings”: two aims that have not been brought into harmony.

passages.c: From Walden. In 1845 Thoreau built a small cabin by Walden Pond in Massachusetts and lived there for two years. Here he explains why.
passages.q: Why did Thoreau go to live in the woods, and what does he think is wrong with ordinary life?
p: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived. I did not wish to live what was not life, living is so dear; nor did I wish to practise resignation, unless it was quite necessary.

I wanted to live deep and suck out all the marrow of life, to live so sturdily and Spartan-like as to put to rout all that was not life, to cut a broad swath and shave close, to drive life into a corner, and reduce it to its lowest terms, and, if it proved to be mean, why then to get the whole and genuine meanness of it, and publish its meanness to the world; or if it were sublime, to know it by experience, and be able to give a true account of it in my next excursion. For most men, it appears to me, are in a strange uncertainty about it, whether it is of the devil or of God, and have somewhat hastily concluded that it is the chief end of man here to "glorify God and enjoy him forever."

Still we live meanly, like ants; though the fable tells us that we were long ago changed into men; like pygmies we fight with cranes; it is error upon error, and clout upon clout, and our best virtue has for its occasion a superfluous and evitable wretchedness. Our life is frittered away by detail. An honest man has hardly need to count more than his ten fingers, or in extreme cases he may add his ten toes, and lump the rest. Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity! I say, let your affairs be as two or three, and not a hundred or a thousand; instead of a million count half a dozen, and keep your accounts on your thumb-nail.

In the midst of this chopping sea of civilized life, such are the clouds and storms and quicksands and thousand-and-one items to be allowed for, that a man has to live, if he would not founder and go to the bottom and not make his port at all, by dead reckoning, and he must be a great calculator indeed who succeeds. Simplify, simplify. Instead of three meals a day, if it be necessary eat but one; instead of a hundred dishes, five; and reduce other things in proportion. Our life is like a German Confederacy, made up of petty states, with its boundary forever fluctuating, so that even a German cannot tell you how it is bounded at any moment.
g: He went to the woods to live deliberately, face only the essentials, and not discover at death that he hadn’t really lived.
He wanted to live intensely and strip life down to learn whether it was mean or sublime, because most people are unsure and have settled the question too hastily.
Yet we live meanly, frittering life away in detail; keep your affairs few: simplicity, simplicity, simplicity.
Modern life has so many hazards and items that you navigate by dead reckoning; simplify: fewer meals, fewer dishes, fewer things.
k: He went to the woods to live deliberately and face only the essential facts of life.
“Our life is frittered away by detail.”
Simplify: let your affairs be as two or three, not a hundred or a thousand.

mc.s: What is Thoreau’s central message here?
o: Strip life down to essentials so you can live it fully and deliberately
Everyone should move to the woods
Eating less is the key to health
mc.e: The woods were his means; the point is living deliberately, which needs simplicity.

mc.s: Why does he compare our life to “a German Confederacy”?
o: To show that a life split into many petty concerns has no clear shape or boundary
To show that life is well organised
mc.e: The Confederacy was a patchwork of small states whose borders kept shifting. So is a life of a thousand small items.

mc.s: Which change best follows Thoreau’s advice for an overloaded executive?
o: Cut to the two or three priorities that matter and drop the rest
Buy a better app to manage all hundred tasks
Work longer hours to fit everything in
Delegate everything and keep the same number of projects
mc.e: “Let your affairs be as two or three, and not a hundred or a thousand.”

v.d: To “live deliberately” is to choose how you live rather than drift.
Frittering is wasting something in small, unnoticed pieces.

gl.dead reckoning: navigating by calculation alone, without landmarks

passages.t: That government is best which governs least
passages.c: From Civil Disobedience (1849). Thoreau had spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax, in protest against slavery and the Mexican–American War.
passages.q: What does Thoreau think government actually achieves, and what does the real work?
p: I heartily accept the motto, "That government is best which governs least"; and I should like to see it acted up to more rapidly and systematically. Carried out, it finally amounts to this, which also I believe--"That government is best which governs not at all"; and when men are prepared for it, that will be the kind of government which they will have. Government is at best but an expedient; but most governments are usually, and all governments are sometimes, inexpedient. The objections which have been brought against a standing army, and they are many and weighty, and deserve to prevail, may also at last be brought against a standing government. The standing army is only an arm of the standing government. The government itself, which is only the mode which the people have chosen to execute their will, is equally liable to be abused and perverted before the people can act through it. Witness the present Mexican war, the work of comparatively a few individuals using the standing government as their tool; for in the outset, the people would not have consented to this measure.

This American government--what is it but a tradition, though a recent one, endeavoring to transmit itself unimpaired to posterity, but each instant losing some of its integrity? It has not the vitality and force of a single living man; for a single man can bend it to his will. It is a sort of wooden gun to the people themselves. But it is not the less necessary for this; for the people must have some complicated machinery or other, and hear its din, to satisfy that idea of government which they have. Governments show thus how successfully men can be imposed upon, even impose on themselves, for their own advantage. It is excellent, we must all allow. Yet this government never of itself furthered any enterprise, but by the alacrity with which it got out of its way. It does not keep the country free.

It does not settle the West. It does not educate. The character inherent in the American people has done all that has been accomplished; and it would have done somewhat more, if the government had not sometimes got in its way. For government is an expedient, by which men would fain succeed in letting one another alone; and, as has been said, when it is most expedient, the governed are most let alone by it. Trade and commerce, if they were not made of india-rubber, would never manage to bounce over obstacles which legislators are continually putting in their way; and if one were to judge these men wholly by the effects of their actions and not partly by their intentions, they would deserve to be classed and punished with those mischievious persons who put obstructions on the railroads.
g: Thoreau accepts that the best government governs least, ultimately not at all, once people are ready; government is a mere expedient, easily abused, as the Mexican war, the work of a few, shows.

The American government is a tradition losing integrity, weaker than one man, a wooden gun; needed only to satisfy people’s idea of government, it has furthered nothing except by getting out of the way.
It doesn’t settle the West or educate; the people’s character did everything; trade bounces over lawmakers’ obstacles, and judged by effects those lawmakers deserve punishment like railway saboteurs.
k: “That government is best which governs not at all”, when people are ready for it.
Government is only an expedient, easily abused by a few, as in the Mexican war.
The people’s character, not government, has done all that was accomplished; government gets in the way.

mc.s: What is Thoreau’s main claim?
o: Government is at best a tool, and the people’s own character accomplishes what matters
mc.e: “The character inherent in the American people has done all that has been accomplished.”

mc.s: What does he mean by calling government “a sort of wooden gun to the people themselves”?
o: It looks like a source of power but has little real force of its own
It is crafted by skilled workers
mc.e: A wooden gun looks like a weapon but cannot fire. “A single man can bend it to his will.”

mc.s: Which example does Thoreau give of government being used as a tool by a few?
mc.e: “The work of comparatively a few individuals using the standing government as their tool.”

o: a means to an end, chosen because it is convenient
v.d: “Government is at best but an expedient”: a practical device, not something valuable in itself.
It furthered enterprise only “by the alacrity with which it got out of its way”.
